questions.prompt: What best defines open search in this chapter?
choices: Collecting as many ideas as possible without ever choosing
Keeping the field of plausible options open long enough before evaluation narrows it
Picking the first option that seems efficient

explanation.gentle: Open search means preserving serious alternatives before judgment starts cutting them down.
explanation.direct: The chapter defines open search as disciplined widening before evaluation, not endless ideation or premature commitment.
explanation.competitive: Keep the field real before the cuts begin.

choices: Because it can make the first workable answer win before comparison happens
Because it always proves the decision maker is careless
Because any fast decision is automatically wrong

explanation.gentle: The first answer can look stronger than it is if the field closes too soon.
explanation.direct: Early lock-in is risky because one candidate may win by arrival time instead of fit.
explanation.competitive: The early favorite can steal the match.

questions.prompt: What do multiple serious options improve later in the process?
choices: They guarantee the newest idea will be best
They strengthen evaluation by making comparison more honest
They remove the need to narrow choices later

explanation.gentle: Several candidates help because tradeoffs become easier to see.
explanation.direct: The chapter values multiple options because evaluation works better when alternatives can be compared directly.
explanation.competitive: Rivals make the later cut smarter.

questions.prompt: A team circles the first plan on the whiteboard and starts debating details before other candidates are named. What is the better move?
choices: Assume the circled plan is best because it appeared first
Pause judgment and add other serious candidates before ranking
Keep one plan only so the team moves faster

explanation.gentle: The field should widen before evaluation starts narrowing it.
explanation.direct: The chapter asks for candidate generation before ranking so the first answer does not win by default.
explanation.competitive: Make the favorite face real rivals.

questions.prompt: In a meeting, each new suggestion gets rejected immediately. According to the chapter, what is going wrong?
choices: Generation and evaluation are collapsing into each other too early
The group needs stranger ideas
The group should commit even faster

explanation.gentle: Search is being cut down before enough candidates can reach the table.
explanation.direct: The chapter protects a separation between generating options and judging them.
explanation.competitive: The cuts started before the bracket filled.

questions.prompt: A student group wants to repeat last year's plan because it feels safe, but they have not named other plausible routes. What should happen first?
choices: Lock in the familiar route because experience makes comparison unnecessary
Widen the option set with other serious candidates before choosing
Wait indefinitely until dozens of ideas appear

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants a broader field before commitment, not automatic repetition or endless delay.
explanation.direct: Open search matters because habit can crowd out better alternatives before they get serious attention.
explanation.competitive: Do not let the incumbent win uncontested.

questions.prompt: What is the possibility space in this chapter?
choices: The wider set of plausible alternatives before the best one is chosen
A list of unrealistic ideas gathered for inspiration
The one option already favored by the group

explanation.gentle: Possibility space means the broader field of plausible routes that exist before narrowing begins.
explanation.direct: The chapter uses possibilities to mean real alternatives still available during disciplined search.
explanation.competitive: It is the field before the cuts.

questions.prompt: Why is novelty not the same as quality?
choices: Because a different option still has to fit the problem better, not merely look new
Because the oldest option is usually correct
Because surprising ideas should always be removed first

explanation.gentle: A new idea helps only if it deserves consideration for fit, not just for surprise.
explanation.direct: The chapter rejects novelty worship because exploration serves judgment, not excitement alone.
explanation.competitive: Different does not automatically hit harder.

questions.prompt: How does broader exploration help evaluation?
choices: It guarantees the final choice will be easy
It gives evaluation real contrast among serious candidates
It removes the need to judge tradeoffs later

explanation.gentle: Evaluation improves when alternatives can be compared against one another.
explanation.direct: A wider field helps because tradeoffs and hidden strengths become easier to see across candidates.
explanation.competitive: Contrast gives the knife a reason.

questions.prompt: According to the chapter's threshold test, when is the search wide enough to start narrowing?
choices: When the first workable answer appears
When the option set has opened enough to avoid trap answers and support real comparison
When every imaginable possibility has been listed

explanation.gentle: The search is wide enough when more than one serious route can be judged honestly.
explanation.direct: The threshold is not endless possibility. It is enough breadth to keep the first plausible answer from winning by default.
explanation.competitive: Start cutting once the field is real.
